[strong]Status:[text] Current, and [strong]partly executed[text]. Written before any UI code existed; the shell, the canvas and the viewport now exist and follow it. The contrast arithmetic on this page is asserted against the real palette by [code]PaletteContrastTests[text] — thirty assertions across twelve tests, including that no state is carried by colour alone. [strong]The colour tables are not asserted in full[text]: the named tokens are real, but several values below are worked examples, rejected candidates or derived ladder steps, and no test tells those apart from tokens. If you change a colour here, change it in [code]SparkPalette[text] and [code]NodeCategory[text] too. [strong]Owner:[text] [code]spark-ui[text] [strong]Last updated:[text] 2026-09-11
[text]This topic is both an end-user reference — [emphasis]why does Spark look like this?[text] — and the
[text]executable specification for the shell, the node canvas renderer and the viewport. Every
[text]colour on this page is a concrete hex value and every contrast ratio is a computed number,
[text]not an assertion. If the implementation and this page disagree, [strong]the page is right[text], and
[text]a pull request that lowers a ratio below its floor is rejected on that ground alone.
level=2 [text]The rule, before anything else

[text]Spark's interface is a dark, soft, physical-feeling surface. Panels look raised. Wells look carved. Buttons look pressed when you press them. That style is [strong]neumorphism[text], and it works by rendering a control in [emphasis]almost the same colour as the surface behind it[text], distinguished only by a paired light-and-dark shadow that suggests a lit, raised object.

[text]That is also exactly why the style has a bad reputation. Low element-to-background contrast is not a defect in careless implementations of neumorphism — it is the definition of the style. So Spark draws a hard line through the middle of it:
[text]### Neumorphism governs surfaces and depth. It never governs legibility.
[text]A soft shadow may say that a thing is [strong]raised[text], [strong]pressed[text], [strong]inset[text] or [strong]floating[text].
[text]A soft shadow may never be the only signal for [strong]text[text], [strong]icons[text], [strong]focus[text], [strong]selection[text],
[strong]error state[text], or [strong]the boundary of a control you have to aim at[text].
[text]Every one of those carries an independent, measurable contrast, and the numbers are in
[link->#4-contrast-rules-with-numbers]§4[text].

[text]The line is drawn there, and not further in, on purpose. A timid neumorphism that keeps every element at high contrast is not a safe neumorphism — it is a flat theme with blurry edges, and it has all of the cost and none of the character. Spark commits to real depth on surfaces: ±9 to ±19 units of L\* between a surface and its shadow pair, which on a dark ground is a great deal. It is strict about where the depth stops.
level=2 [text]1. Principles

[strong]1. Depth is a surface property; legibility is a content property, and they are never traded against each other.[text] The moment a shadow is doing work that a contrast ratio should be doing, the design has failed, because a shadow's readability depends on the monitor, the ambient light, the colour profile and the viewer's eyes, and a contrast ratio does not.

[strong]2. A state change may add a signal or raise contrast. It may never lower it.[text] This is stricter than WCAG requires, and it is what makes a soft, shifting, hover-responsive surface safe to use everywhere without auditing each case individually — the audit is discharged once, by the rule.

[strong]3. Colour is never the only carrier of meaning.[text] Every semantic state pairs a colour with a glyph, a stroke, a position or a word. Roughly one in twelve of Spark's male users has a colour-vision deficiency, and every user has a bad monitor some of the time.

[strong]4. Two roles, two vocabularies: fills identify, strokes report.[text] A node's fill says [emphasis]what kind of node this is[text] (its library category). A stroke, ring or badge says [emphasis]what is happening to it[text] (selected, evaluating, errored, frozen). Because the two never share a pixel role, a green node body and a green wire can coexist without either becoming ambiguous.

[strong]5. The canvas is drawn by hand, so its style must survive being drawn by hand at 2,000 nodes and 60 fps.[text] [link->../../adr/0013-immediate-mode-node-canvas.md]ADR-0013[text] makes the canvas one immediate-mode control over a spatial index, and drops to a level-of-detail representation below 40% zoom. Every canvas cue in this document declares the zoom at which it is dropped and what carries its meaning afterwards.

[strong]6. Restraint is the aesthetic.[text] Spark is a tool people stare at for eight hours while thinking about something else. Motion is short, colour is used sparingly, and nothing moves that the user did not move.
level=2 [text]2. The palette
level=3 [text]2.1 One theme in v1

[strong]Spark v1 ships a dark theme only.[text] There is no light theme, no automatic theme switching and no user colour customisation in 0.1. Shipping one theme properly is worth more than shipping two badly, and a neumorphic system is the worst possible candidate for a naive colour inversion — see [link->#27-what-a-light-theme-would-cost]§2.7[text].
[text]Token names are deliberately theme-neutral ([code]surface.base[text], not [code]grey.800[text]) precisely so that a second theme is a value swap rather than a rename.
level=3 [text]2.2 The surface ladder

[text]Every surface in the product is one of these, and every interactive surface has a [strong]state ladder[text] of successively darker steps used by hover, press and selection (see [link->#5-interaction-states]§5[text]). Steps are roughly −3 L\* apart.

level=3 [text]2.5 Borders, accent and semantics

[strong]Never a control boundary.[text] 1.30:1 on [code]surface.base[text] and that is fine, because it is never load-bearing. | [code]border.control ; [code]#7C8595 ; [text]The boundary token. Every control whose extent must be judged, and every node outline. ≥3.35:1 against every surface in the palette. | [code]border.strong ; [code]#9AA2B1 ; [text]Table rules, the active dock edge, anything that needs to read as structural. | [code]accent ; [code]#A98BFF ; [text]Selection, focus, active tab, primary action, the evaluating indicator | [code]accent.hover ; [code]#C0A8FF ; [text]Accent fill under a pointer | [code]accent.press ; [code]#D4C4FF ; [text]Accent fill while pressed | [code]focus.ring ; [code]#CDBCFF ; [text]The keyboard focus ring | [code]focus.contour ; [code]#0C0E13 ; [text]The 1 px dark separator on both sides of the focus ring | [code]state.error ; [code]#FF7B82 ; [text]Errors, refused connections | [code]state.warning ; [code]#F0A63C ; [text]Warnings, lossy conversions | [code]state.success ; [code]#5FD39A ; [text]Success, valid connections | [code]state.info ; [code]#68B6F2 ; [text]Information, hints
[text]**Decision V1 — the type-compatibility wire colours are the semantic tokens, not a
[text]parallel set.**
[text]When you drag a wire, the graph engine reports whether the connection is accepted, accepted
[text]with a lossy conversion, or refused. Those three states are drawn in [code]state.success[text],
[code]state.warning[text] and [code]state.error[text] — the same three hexes used by node error badges and
[text]diagnostic messages. The rejected alternative was a fourth, wire-only ramp of green/amber/red
[text]chosen to sit "beside" the semantics without colliding. It was rejected because two nearly
[text]identical reds in one product is worse than one red used in two roles: users would have to
[text]learn which red meant what, and the near-match would read as a rendering bug. Principle 4
[text]makes the reuse safe — semantic colours appear only on **strokes, rings, glyphs and message
[text]text**, never as a fill, and the three drag colours appear only on the wire being dragged and
[text]the port under the cursor, only while the mouse button is down. A cursor glyph ([code]✓[text], [code]≈[text], [code]✕[text])
[text]accompanies each, so the meaning survives colour blindness and monochrome capture.
level=3 [text]2.6 The accent hue is substitutable at fixed luminance

[code]accent[text] is the one token in this document that is a brand choice rather than a technical one. Violet was chosen because it is the only saturated hue that does not land inside the red–amber– green–blue bands already claimed by the semantic set, and because a calm accent keeps the loud colours available for things that are actually urgent.
[text]If the brand wants a different hue, [strong]substitute one of these and not a single ratio in this document changes[text], because they are matched on relative luminance:

rows=5 | [text]Option ; [text]Hex ; [text]Relative luminance Y ; [text]On [code]surface.base ; [text]On [code]canvas.bg ; [code]text.inverse[text] on it | [strong]Violet (chosen) ; [code]#A98BFF ; [text]0.3412 ; [text]5.57:1 ; [text]6.43:1 ; [text]6.61:1 | [text]Cyan ; [code]#2FB4C4 ; [text]0.3723 ; [text]6.02:1 ; [text]6.95:1 ; [text]7.14:1 | [text]Magenta ; [code]#EE79BE ; [text]0.3557 ; [text]5.78:1 ; [text]6.67:1 ; [text]6.86:1 | [text]Amber ; [code]#CE9C36 ; [text]0.3717 ; [text]6.01:1 ; [text]6.93:1 ; [text]7.13:1

[text]The constraint on any substitute is stated as a number rather than a taste: [strong]Y between 0.33 and 0.38, and a hue at least 40° away from every semantic hue.[text] Amber is inside that band on luminance but fails the hue clause against [code]state.warning[text]; it is listed for completeness and should not be chosen.
level=3 [text]2.7 What a light theme would cost
[text]Not an inversion. Specifically:
[strong]The depth budget flips sides.[text] On a light base the [emphasis]shadow[text] has all the headroom and the

[emphasis]highlight[text] has almost none, which is the exact mirror of [link->#28-the-hard-part-neumorphic-depth-on-a-dark-ground]§2.8[text]. The 1 px lit lip would become a 1 px shadowed underhang, and the blur radii would shrink.
[strong]Every chromatic token must be re-picked, not darkened.[text] [code]accent[text] at 5.57:1 on [code]#23272F

[text]gives about 1.9:1 on a light [code]#ECEFF4[text]. Accent, all four semantics and all ten category colours need new values, and the category set is the hard one because a light theme compresses the usable luminance band for ten mutually distinguishable hues.
[strong]The wire casing and core swap roles[text] ([link->#75-wires]§7.5[text]): a light casing under a dark core.
[strong]The hover direction reverses.[text] On light surfaces with dark text, hover must [emphasis]lighten
[text]([link->#51-the-hover-rule-and-why-it-inverts-the-usual-move]§5.1[text] explains the invariant that both directions serve).
[strong]The 3D viewport needs its own decision[text], because a light ground changes the shading model,
[text]not just the background colour.
[text]That is a body of work, not a stylesheet. It is out of scope for 0.1 and this section exists so that the size of it is known before someone promises it.
level=3 [text]2.8 The hard part: neumorphic depth on a dark ground
[text]This is the single practical problem that makes dark neumorphism harder than light neumorphism, and a specification that skips it is decoration rather than engineering.

[strong]The shadow is the constrained side, not the highlight.[text] The intuition runs the other way — "there is no room to go lighter on a dark theme" — and it is wrong. The classic light-neumorphic base is around [code]#E0E5EC[text], at L\[emphasis] ≈ 90: the highlight has about 10 units of L\[text] above it and the shadow has about 90 below. Spark's base is at L\[emphasis] 15.56: the highlight has about 84 units above it and the shadow has [emphasis]15.56[text]*. Depth is read primarily from occlusion — from the dark side — so dark neumorphism starves the cue that actually does the work.
[text]Three consequences follow, and each has a countermeasure written into this specification.

[strong](a) The base must be lifted off black.[text] [code]surface.base[text] is [code]#23272F[text], not [code]#121212[text]. That is deliberate and it costs contrast against text, which is why the base sits where it does and not higher. The rule is: [strong]a surface that carries elevation must leave at least 10 units of L\* between itself and the shadow floor.[text] [code]surface.base[text] leaves 11.59, [code]surface.raised[text] leaves 15.30, [code]surface.float[text] leaves 19.41. [code]canvas.bg[text] and [code]bg.void[text] deliberately carry [emphasis]no[text] elevation of their own, which is what lets them sit lower.

[strong](b) The shadow must not bottom out at pure black.[text] [code]depth.lo.float[text] is [code]#07080B[text] (L\[emphasis] 2.20), not `#000000`. A pure-black shadow on an OLED or a well-calibrated panel reads as a hole punched through the interface rather than as an occluded surface, and it also removes the last of the gradient's room to fall off. The floor is L\[text] ≥ 2.

[strong](c) The lit side has to stop being a blur and become a line.[text] A wide, soft, light-on-dark highlight does not read as a lit surface; it reads as an emissive rim — a glow — because matte dark materials do not produce broad specular highlights in the real world. Worse, a glow is exactly the visual language reserved for focus, so a big highlight competes with the one cue that must never be ambiguous. So Spark spends almost all of the lit-side budget on a [strong]1 px lip[text] ([code]lip.rest[text], [code]#3E4654[text], +10.25 L\*) along the top and left edges of a raised surface, and only a narrow 6 px blur behind it. Crisp lines read as lit edges; broad ones read as lamps.

[text]There is a fourth problem that is purely technical: [strong]banding[text]. A blurred shadow falling from [code]#0C0E13[text] to [code]#23272F[text] traverses about 23 8-bit code values over 12 px. That is visibly stepped on a large surface. Every shadow gradient in Spark is dithered with 1.5% monochrome noise applied at composite time; this is cheap, invisible as texture, and removes Mach banding entirely.

[text]The pleasing part of (c) is that it is also the fix for the interaction problem. Because the lit-side budget lives in a 1 px line rather than in the surface fill, [strong]hover can brighten the lip without brightening anything that sits behind text[text] — which is precisely what [link->#51-the-hover-rule-and-why-it-inverts-the-usual-move]§5.1[text] needs.
level=2 [text]3. Elevation
[text]Four levels. Not five, not nine.

[text]Offsets and blurs are in device-independent pixels at 100% scale. The light source is fixed at the [strong]top-left[text], so lit edges are up-and-left and shadows fall down-and-right, everywhere, with no exceptions. Blur radii are drawn from the fixed set [strong]{5, 6, 12, 16, 28}[text] so that the canvas renderer can cache shadow sprites per size bucket rather than running a real Gaussian blur per node — at 2,000 nodes the difference is the frame budget.
level=3 [text]E0 — Flat
[text]No shadow, no lip. The surface is simply a fill.
[text]Used by: [code]canvas.bg[text], [code]bg.void[text], panel backgrounds, table rows at rest, [strong]every disabled control[text], and every canvas element below 73% zoom.
level=3 [text]E1 — Inset
[text]The surface is carved into its parent.

[text]Used by: text fields, the search box, slider tracks, the list well, tab strips, the [strong]pressed[text] state of any E2 control, and the [strong]off[text] state of the node preview toggle.

[text]The default for anything you can click.

[text]E3 is the only level with an outline in its base definition, because a floating surface can land on top of anything — including a bright node header — and the shadow alone cannot be relied on to separate it from an arbitrary backdrop.
level=2 [text]4. Contrast rules, with numbers
level=3 [text]4.1 The floors

rows=8 | [text]What ; [text]Floor ; [text]Source | [text]Body text, and any text below 18 px regular / 14 px bold ; [strong]4.5:1 ; [text]WCAG 2.2 AA, SC 1.4.3 | [text]Large text: ≥18 px regular or ≥14 px semibold ; [strong]3:1 ; [text]WCAG 2.2 AA, SC 1.4.3 | [text]Icons and glyphs that carry meaning ; [strong]3:1 ; [text]WCAG 2.2 AA, SC 1.4.11 | [text]The boundary of a control whose extent must be judged ; [strong]3:1 ; [text]WCAG 2.2 AA, SC 1.4.11 | [text]Focus indicator, against [strong]both[text] of its neighbours ; [strong]3:1 ; [text]WCAG 2.2 AA, SC 1.4.11 / 2.4.13 | [text]Node fill against the canvas at LOD ; [strong]3:1 ; [text]Local rule; a node is a control | [text]A wire against whatever it crosses ; [strong]3:1 ; [text]Local rule

[strong]Spark applies the 4.5:1 body floor to large text as well.[text] The 3:1 allowance exists because big glyphs have thicker strokes; but Spark's largest routine text is 15 px, the scale tops out at 28 px for empty states, and the saving would apply almost nowhere. Holding one number is simpler to review than holding two, and no pairing in this palette needed the relaxation.

[strong]`text.disabled` is held to 4.5:1 as well.[text] WCAG exempts disabled controls. Spark does not take the exemption, because "you cannot use this" and "you cannot read this" are different statements and users routinely need to read a disabled field to work out how to enable it.
level=3 [text]4.2 What the floors do [emphasis]not[text] cover
[text]Stated up front so it is a scope definition and not a later excuse. Three categories are exempt, each with a replacement guarantee:
[strong]Decorative dividers[text] ([code]border.hairline[text], 1.30:1 on [code]surface.base[text]). Exempt because they
[text]separate content that is already separated by layout. They may never be the only boundary of an interactive control; [code]border.control[text] exists for that.
[strong]Depth pairs and lips[text] ([code]lip.rest[text], 1.41:1 on [code]surface.raised[text]). Exempt by Principle 1 — they
[text]are the style, not the signal. Every control they decorate is identifiable without them.
[strong]Shaded 3D geometry and the viewport grid.[text] The viewport renders a scene, not a document.

[code]grid.minor[text] sits at 1.26:1 against the viewport background on purpose. Everything [emphasis]overlaid[text] on the scene — selection outlines, axis labels, dimension text, warnings — is UI and is fully in scope. The single deliberate exception inside the scene is ghosted geometry, and [link->#84-ghosted-geometry-the-one-declared-exception]§8.4[text] states it as an exception with its number and its second signal.

[strong]Where `border.control` is required, and where it is not.[text] SC 1.4.11 requires a 3:1 boundary where the boundary is needed to [emphasis]identify[text] the control. [strong]every node on the canvas[text], because a node's extent is what you aim at, drag by and connect

level=2 [text]5. Interaction states
level=3 [text]5.1 The hover rule, and why it inverts the usual move

[text]Principle 2 says a state change may not lower contrast. On a dark theme carrying light text, the usual dark-theme hover — [emphasis]brighten the surface[text] — does exactly that: it moves the surface towards the text and the ratio falls. The usual neumorphic hover has the same problem for the same reason.
[text]So the rule is stated in a form that is direction-independent:
[strong]Hover moves a surface *away* from the colour of the text on it. Never towards it.
[text]- A dark surface with light text gets [strong]darker[text] on hover.
[text]- A bright fill with dark text (accent buttons, node headers, semantic badges) gets
[text]  [strong]brighter[text] on hover.
[text]In both cases the ratio rises. There is no third case.

[text]The felt sense of "coming forward" is then supplied by the two things that are [emphasis]not[text] behind text: the [strong]lip[text] brightens from [code]lip.rest[text] [code]#3E4654[text] to [code]lip.hover[text] [code]#8674D6[text], and the [strong]elevation[text] increases — the E2 shadow offset grows from +3,+4 to +4,+6 and its blur from 12 to 16. That is physically coherent as well: lifting an object off a surface casts a longer shadow and does not require the object's own face to catch more light.
[strong]Explicitly forbidden[text], in review, in code, in design files:
[text]darkening a surface [emphasis]towards[text] the text on it (light text on a lightening surface, or dark text
[text]on a darkening one);
[text]lowering text opacity to signal any state whatsoever;
[text]tinting a fill with [code]accent[text] or a semantic colour underneath text — see
[link->#54-selected]§5.4[text] for what to do instead;
[text]signalling hover only by a change in blur radius, which is invisible at small sizes and on
[text]low-DPI panels.

level=3 [text]5.4 Selected

[text]Selection never tints a fill that sits behind text. [code]accent[text] at 14% over [code]surface.base[text] produces [code]#36354C[text], on which [code]text.primary[text] reads 10.85:1 — down from 13.69:1 at rest. It is still far above the floor, and it is still forbidden, because Principle 2 is an invariant and not a budget.
[text]Selection is instead signalled by three stacked cues:

[text]1. the fill steps [strong]down[text] the ladder (contrast rises); 2. a [strong]3 px `accent` spine[text] on the leading edge for rows, or a [strong]2 px `accent` ring[text] for nodes and canvas objects — 6.37:1 against the selected row fill, 5.30:1 against [code]node.body[text]; 3. the label moves from weight 400 to weight 500.
[text]Accent tints are permitted only where there is no text over them: the marquee rectangle on empty canvas, the filled portion of a slider track, and progress fills.

[strong]Multi-selection[text] uses the same ring on every member. The [strong]anchor[text] — the item keyboard operations act from, and the one whose properties the inspector shows — additionally carries four 6 px [code]accent[text] corner ticks. Ticks were chosen over a brighter ring because they are a [emphasis]shape[text] difference: they survive monochrome rendering, colour blindness and a bad monitor.
level=3 [text]5.5 Disabled
[text]Disabled is signalled by [strong]the removal of depth[text], not by the removal of contrast.
[text]Elevation drops to [strong]E0[text]. Nothing raised, nothing inset, no lip. In a system where depth means
[text]interactive, flatness reads immediately as "not that".
[text]The fill becomes [code]surface.sunken[text]; text becomes [code]text.disabled[text], which is still ≥4.56:1
[text]everywhere.
[text]Accent and semantic colour is [strong]removed[text], not faded — a disabled primary button is a flat grey
[text]button, not a translucent violet one.
[text]There is [strong]no hover response at all[text], which is the single clearest confirmation a pointer user
[text]can get.
[text]The cursor becomes [code]not-allowed[text], and the control is removed from the tab order but keeps its
[text]accessible name and a [code]disabled[text] state so a screen reader announces it.
[text]Five independent signals, none of them a contrast reduction.
level=3 [text]5.6 Error
[text]Error is never colour alone. Every error state carries [strong]all three[text] of:

[text]1. a 2 px [code]state.error[text] stroke on the control's boundary (5.00–6.91:1 against every surface); 2. a [code]✕[text] glyph, drawn as a shape and not as a font glyph so it survives font fallback; 3. a message in words, in [code]state.error[text] on the surface, at ≥5.00:1.

[text]Warnings use [code]state.warning[text] and a [code]⚠[text] glyph and are otherwise identical. This mirrors the engine: [link->lacing.md]`concepts.lacing`[text] §2.12 distinguishes an Error, which produces no output, from a Warning, which produces output with caveats, and the interface must make the same distinction visible without the user having to read the diagnostic code.

[strong]A warning message carries the triangle before its words[text] — in a banner, in a pane, anywhere the shell warns in a sentence rather than on a node. The client's rule, 2026-09-11: [emphasis]always add warning triangle before the message[text]. It is [code]SparkWarningGlyph[text], drawn as a path in [code]state.warning[text] through the [code]PathIcon.warning[text] style, 16 px on the first line of the text. A new warning writes [code]Classes="warning"[text] and gets it, rather than drawing its own:
lang=xml lines=4
[text]Informational text — the status bar, [emphasis]Nothing selected[text] — does not carry one, because a glyph on everything means nothing.
level=2 [text]6. Keyboard focus

[text]A focus ring drawn as a soft glow is invisible to exactly the people who need it, on exactly the displays they are most likely to be using. Spark's focus indicator is a hard geometric shape with a guaranteed ratio on both of its sides.
[strong]The focus sandwich.[text] 4 px total, drawn [strong]outside[text] the control's bounds with a 2 px gap:

rows=4 | [text]Layer ; [text]Width ; [text]Colour | [text]Inner separator ; [text]1 px ; [code]focus.contour[text] [code]#0C0E13 | [text]Ring ; [text]2 px ; [code]focus.ring[text] [code]#CDBCFF | [text]Outer separator ; [text]1 px ; [code]focus.contour[text] [code]#0C0E13

[text]The two dark separators exist so that the ring's 3:1 requirement holds regardless of what it touches. Against [code]focus.contour[text] the ring reads [strong]11.24:1[text]; [code]focus.contour[text] reads [strong]7.19:1[text] against an [code]accent[text] fill, [strong]11.46:1[text] against the brightest node header, and [strong]17.66:1[text] against [code]text.primary[text]. So a focused button on a panel, a focused item inside a selected accent row, and a focused port on a gold [code]Input[text] node are all covered by the same four pixels, with no per-case reasoning.

[text]The ring alone, without the sandwich, already reads 7.27–10.06:1 against every surface in the palette ([link->#46-non-text-boundaries]§4.6[text]). The sandwich exists for the arbitrary backdrops: node headers, geometry in the viewport, and floating layers.
[strong]Rules that go with it:
[strong]Focus is independent of hover.[text] A hovered control shows its hover state; a focused control
[text]shows the ring; a hovered [emphasis]and[text] focused control shows both. Neither substitutes for the other, and moving the mouse never removes a keyboard focus ring.
[strong]Focus is independent of selection.[text] In the library, [code]Down[text] moves focus without changing
[text]selection; the focused row shows the ring, the selected row shows the accent spine, and one row can show both.
[strong]Focus is never shown by colour alone.[text] It has a position (outside the bounds), a geometry
[text](4 px, hard-edged, following the control's corner radius) and a value.
[strong]Focus is never shown by a glow, a blur, a shadow or an elevation change.[text] Listed as a
[text]prohibition in [link->#11-what-this-style-is-not-allowed-to-do]§11[text] because it is the specific failure this section exists to prevent.
[strong]Focus is visible on first `Tab`.[text] There is no focus-visible heuristic that hides the ring
[text]from pointer users and then fails to bring it back.
[strong]On the canvas[text], where there are no Avalonia controls to inherit focus behaviour from

[text](ADR-0013), the renderer draws the same sandwich around the focused node, port or wire, and scrolls it into view. This is explicitly part of the M8 accessibility pass and is specified here so that pass has something to implement rather than to invent.

[text]The hardest surface in the product, because it is drawn by our own renderer rather than by Avalonia (ADR-0013), because several hundred nodes are on screen at once, and because below 40% zoom nodes degrade to plain category-coloured rectangles with no text at all.

[strong]The header is also the rename target[text] ([code]E8-T68[text]). Double-clicking it opens a text box over the title with the whole title selected, because the commonest rename replaces the name outright. On a code block this beats the click that opens the source editor — a rule with an exception for one node kind is a rule nobody can learn, and the cost is the one band of a block that is not source.

[strong]A node is as wide as twice its wider half[text] ([code]E8-T70[text]), not as wide as its widest row. Those are different numbers, and the difference is where the split falls: a row measured as a sum can be wide enough overall and still put an input's type label across the middle, which is what happened the moment the middle became a line. Each half is the port inset, the side's tab, the gap, the type label and half the row gutter.

[strong]The body is divided down the middle[text] ([code]E8-T67[text]), and what the line says is that a node's two columns mean different things: the left edge is where wires arrive, the right edge is where they leave. It is [code]border.hairline[text], the palette's quietest line, because a divider [emphasis]inside[text] a surface must not read as an edge [emphasis]between[text] two things. The output half is washed 8% black — a step smaller than one rung of the body ladder, so it reads as a tint and not as a second surface. [strong]The wash darkens rather than lightens, and that direction is Principle 2 rather than taste[text]: body text on a node is light, so darkening the surface under it can only raise contrast. Neither is drawn below 67% zoom, which is where the body begins lerping towards the category colour and where there are no port labels left to separate.

[text]The header is the load-bearing element and it does four jobs at once: it names the node, it carries the category identity, it provides the node's most visible boundary against the canvas (every category reads 5.39–10.26:1 there), and it is the one part of a node whose hover [emphasis]brightens[text], because it carries dark text.
[text]**Decision V2 — the node header is a full-strength category fill with dark text, not a muted
[text]band with light text.**
[text]The rejected alternative was to composite the category colour at about 30% over [code]node.body[text],
[text]giving a subdued band that could carry [code]text.primary[text] like the rest of the interface. It reads
[text]better as a single node and fails as a canvas: a 30% band sits between 1.90:1 ([code]cat.script[text]) and
[text]2.46:1 ([code]cat.input[text]) against [code]canvas.bg[text], all of them below the 3:1 floor, so a node has no
[text]visible boundary of its own, the category is barely perceptible
[text]at 60% zoom, and the LOD transition at 40% becomes a jarring jump from a muted grey-blue node
[text]to a saturated blue rectangle. A full-strength header makes the LOD transition [emphasis]continuous[text] —
[text]the category colour's share of the node's area simply grows from about 20% to 100% as you zoom
[text]out — and it puts dark text on a bright fill, which is the one place in a dark interface where
[text]hover can brighten without violating Principle 2.
level=3 [text]7.2 Category colour identity

[strong]A node on the canvas is grey until somebody colours it.[text] That was not always so: every node used to take its library category's fill, and the client asked for the Dynamo behaviour instead. The reasoning is worth keeping, because it is about what colour is [emphasis]for[text] — a canvas where every node is coloured by its category spends all of its colour saying [emphasis]what kind of node this is[text], which is a fact the node's own name already states. Grey gives the colour back to the user, so that a coloured node means [strong]somebody chose to mark this one[text]. The palette below is what they may choose from, and [code]cat.custom[text] grey is what a node has until they do.

[strong]What this costs is the silhouette.[text] ADR-0013 degrades a node to a plain coloured rectangle below 40% zoom, and colour was the only thing left carrying identity at that scale; a canvas of grey rectangles carries none. That is a real loss and it is the trade the request makes: at that zoom a graph is a shape to navigate rather than a thing to read, and the colours somebody applied themselves are the ones that survive it — which is arguably what they were for.
[strong]The library panel still colours its rows by category.[text] [emphasis]What kind of node is this[text] is a question the library exists to answer, and that is where the answer belongs.
[text]Category colours are chosen for mutual separation and for contrast against the canvas, not for prettiness.

level=3 [text]7.3 How depth degrades with zoom

[text]A blurred shadow stops reading as depth once its blur radius falls below about 4 device pixels; below that it is not a shadow, it is a smear that costs fill rate. [text]A single mid-grey stroke chosen to "work against both" cannot be made to work. [text]Port geometry encodes the declared rank of the port, which is the concept [link->lacing.md]`concepts.lacing`[text] §2.2 says everything else depends on. Making it visible on the canvas means a user can see [emphasis]why[text] a node replicated without opening anything.

[code]port.rest[text] is [code]#8A93A2[text] (4.59:1 on [code]node.body[text], 5.57:1 on [code]canvas.bg[text]) for an unconnected port and [code]port.connected[text] is [code]#C6CDDA[text] — the same value as [code]wire.core[text], so a wire visually terminates in its port rather than stopping next to it.

[text]The [strong]hit target is 14 × 14 px regardless of the drawn size[text], and it does not shrink below 10 px of screen space as you zoom out. Ports are the smallest thing anyone has to aim at in the product.

[strong]A port is a lozenge carrying its own name, and the whole lozenge is the target.[text] It is an inset well in [code]surface.sunken[text] — a port is a socket, something a wire goes [emphasis]into[text], so it reads as a hole in the node rather than as a button on it — flush with the node's edge, 15 px tall, and [strong]as wide as the longest name on its side[text] with 8 px either side, never wider than two fifths of the node. The width is per [emphasis]side[text] and not per port ([code]E8-T66[text]): a lozenge is a target as much as a label, and a column of targets that all begin at the same edge and stop at three different ones is harder to aim down than a column of equal ones. The two sides are measured separately — they face each other across the body, and matching them to each other is a rule nobody asked for. A connected one fills 45% towards [code]port.connected[text]; the hovered one takes the same [code]accent[text] outline everything hoverable on this canvas takes. [strong]The point of the shape is the target[text]: clicking the word [code]radius[text] starts the wire that [code]radius[text] wants, which is a fifty-pixel target instead of a five-pixel one. Below the zoom that draws port names, the lozenges go and the discs are all that is left, because a lozenge with no room for a word in it is a rectangle that means nothing.

[strong]The port disc is 7 px and its hit target is 18.[text] It was 5 px over 14 and a user reported that the dots were hard to pick — which is the one complaint a canvas cannot argue with, because a port is the smallest thing anybody has to aim at and it is where every wire starts. The disc grew with the target rather than only the target growing: an invisible margin that works is still a control that looks wrong.

[strong]Beside the port name, in `text.muted` at 10 px, is the type the port wants.[text] [code]center  Point3d[text]. [code]radius  number[text]. [code]sweepAngle  degrees[text]. Without it a port is a word and not an instruction: a user looking at [code]Circle.FromCenterRadius[text] for the first time has no way to learn from the node that [code]center[text] wants a point, and the two places that would have told them — the library entry's signature and the colour of a wire being dragged at it — are both somewhere other than where the question is asked. [code]text.muted[text] reads 6.28:1 on [code]node.body[text], and it is the token this design language already reserves for units and counts, which is the register a type annotation belongs to.
[text]Three rules keep it from becoming noise.
[strong]The name wins the row.[text] The type is a step smaller and a step dimmer, and it is dropped a
[text]level of detail before the name ([link->#73-how-depth-degrades-with-zoom]§7.3[text]).
[strong]A name that already says the type does not say it twice.[text] An output called [code]circle[text] returning

[text]a [code]Circle[text] is drawn as [code]circle[text], and so is a [code]curves[text] input taking a list of [code]Curve[text]. The suppression is on the words, so [code]points[text] returning [code]Point3d[text] still shows the type — the kernel type really is [code]Point3d[text], and somebody hunting the library for one is better off knowing.
[strong]Listness is not repeated.[text] Whether a port wants one value or many is the ring in the table
[text]above, and the type names the element. A node that said both would be spending width to say the same thing twice.

[text]The type is drawn [strong]only when the row has room for it[text] — a node is sized before any text has been measured, so what a row cannot fit it does without, rather than overlapping the port name opposite.
level=3 [text]7.6.1 The creation box

[text]Double-clicking empty canvas opens a search box at the pointer ([link->finding-nodes.md]`concepts.finding-nodes`[text]). It is [code]surface.float[text] with a 1 px [code]border.control[text] frame and a soft drop shadow — the elevation [link->#3-elevation]§3[text] reserves for menus, popups and autocomplete — because it floats over a canvas that sits only 1.2:1 away from it and needs an edge to be readable at all.

[strong]It is a real Avalonia control, and it is the first one.[text] Every node on this canvas is drawn rather than instantiated (ADR-0013), and the exception the decision always allowed for is the thing currently being interacted with: one control, in screen space, over the drawing. The in-place node editor belongs in the same layer when it arrives.

[text]Two behaviours are part of the design rather than of the implementation. The box is [strong]clamped inside the canvas[text], so a double-click near an edge does not open something half unreachable. And the node lands at the point that was [strong]double-clicked[text], not at the pointer's position when Enter was pressed — the wheel can pan and zoom while the box is open, and a node arriving somewhere other than where it was asked for is the kind of small betrayal that makes a gesture feel unreliable.
level=3 [text]7.6.2 The preview bubble

[strong]A node that has run carries a bubble under it, and it has three states[text] ([code]E8-T72[text]). Collapsed it is a 20 px strip, the node's own width, naming the type that came out — [code]Circle[text], [code]Rgba[text], [code]Brep[text] — or the node's rank line when its output declares no type. A triangle at the right opens it onto the rank line and the value, which is what the bubble has always shown (§7.6, [code]E8-T10[text]). A pin beside that triangle keeps it open after the node stops being selected.

[strong]The pin is what the bubble was missing rather than a convenience.[text] Before it there were two states and nothing between them: a value that went away the moment you looked elsewhere, or a [code]Watch[text] node wired into the graph — which is a change to the [emphasis]document[text] to answer a question about [emphasis]looking[text]. So a pin records no undo step, changes no wire, and is not saved: a bubble left open is the same kind of fact as which node is selected.

[strong]Closing a pinned bubble unpins it, and pinning a closed one opens it.[text] A pin keeps an [emphasis]open[text] bubble, so a pinned closed one would be invisible state making a node behave differently from its neighbours for no visible reason — and a pin on a strip would keep a word on screen when the thing worth keeping is the value.

[strong]A node, the gap under it and its bubble are one region for the pointer[text] ([code]E8-T73[text]). The bubble is drawn six units clear of the node so the two read as separate things, and those six units are the ground a pointer crosses on the way to the toggle — so the hover treats the three as contiguous. That generosity is for hovering only: a [emphasis]press[text] in the gap belongs to the canvas and starts a marquee like any other press on nothing.

[strong]It is capped at eight wrapped lines.[text] A bubble is a glance; a list of a thousand points wraps to hundreds of lines and covers the graph it is annotating. The properties pane holds the whole value, and says how much it cut.
level=3 [text]7.7 Frozen, preview off, and not evaluated
[text]Three states that all mean "this node is not currently contributing", and all three are easy to implement badly by fading the node until it cannot be read.

[strong]Frozen[text] desaturates the header to the grey of [emphasis]identical relative luminance[text] — [code]cat.point[text] [code]#5AA2EA[text] becomes [code]#9E9E9E[text], [code]cat.math[text] [code]#DE7B50[text] becomes [code]#969696[text]. Because the substitution is luminance-preserving, header text contrast is unchanged to within a hundredth: 6.58 → 6.62 and 5.96 → 6.00. The state is carried by the loss of [emphasis]hue[text], which costs no contrast at all, plus a [code]⏸[text] glyph and a solid outline.

[strong]Preview off[text] — the node computes, but its geometry is not drawn in the viewport — changes no colour whatever. The preview toggle moves from E2 raised to E1 inset, its glyph becomes eye-off, and the node outline becomes dashed. Depth is exactly the right vocabulary for this, because nothing about it concerns legibility.

[strong]Not evaluated[text] is the grey state that [link->lacing.md]`concepts.lacing`[text] §2.5 describes: when an upstream node errors, downstream nodes are greyed as [emphasis]not evaluated[text] rather than flooded with errors of their own. It uses the frozen desaturation, plus a dashed outline, plus a [code]○[text] glyph, plus a body at L−2 — which [emphasis]raises[text] text contrast to 15.12:1. A user must still be able to read a node that did not run, because reading it is how they work out what should have run.

[strong]Evaluating[text] is the only animated state: a 2 px [code]accent[text] stroke travelling around the node outline on a 900 ms linear loop, plus a progress glyph in the header. Under reduced motion the stroke becomes a static, complete [code]accent[text] ring and the glyph becomes [code]…[text]. The information is retained; only the movement is removed. Outside the canvas's animation budget - below 60% zoom, or with more than 400 nodes visible (§10.2) - the travelling stroke is replaced by the static ring for every user, because animating hundreds of outlines is not affordable inside the 60 fps target ADR-0013 sets. This paragraph said 55% until the stroke was built ([code]E3-T14[text]); §10.2's budget is the stricter of the two and the one the canvas already enforced, so it is the one that holds.
level=3 [text]7.8 Groups and notes

[text]A [strong]group[text] is [code]canvas.group[text] [code]#1E222A[text] with a 1 px [code]border.control[text] frame and a title bar in [code]surface.base[text] carrying [code]text.secondary[text] at 9.97:1. The fill sits at 1.08:1 against the canvas on purpose — a group is a region, not an object, and its frame and title are what identify it.

[text]A [strong]note[text] is E2 on [code]surface.raised[text] with [code]text.primary[text] at 12.30:1, and it obeys the ordinary state ladder. Notes are read, so they are held to text rules, not to canvas rules.
level=2 [text]8. The 3D viewport
level=3 [text]8.1 Ground and grid

rows=5 | [text]Token ; [text]Hex ; [text]Notes | [code]viewport.top ; [code]#1B1F26 ; [text]Top of a vertical gradient | [code]viewport.bottom ; [code]#14171D ; [text]Bottom of the gradient | [code]grid.minor ; [code]#2A313C ; [text]1 model unit; 1.26:1 against the ground | [code]grid.major ; [code]#3A414D ; [text]every 10 units; 1.60:1 against the ground

[text]The background is a gradient rather than a flat fill because a flat dark field gives the eye no horizon and makes a rotating model feel like it is floating in nothing; the gradient supplies a weak up-direction for free. It is dithered with the same 1.5% noise as the shadows, for the same banding reason.
[text]It is deliberately not black. Shaded geometry needs somewhere to put its own shadow side, and on a black ground the dark faces of a mesh merge with the void and the silhouette reads as a hole.

[text]The grid ratios are low on purpose and are covered by the exemption in [link->#42-what-the-floors-do-not-cover]§4.2[text]: a grid is a scene element that must be legible when you look for it and invisible when you do not. Both grids fade with distance.

This is the one place where an outside convention beats internal consistency: every CAD and DCC tool an AEC user has ever opened uses this mapping, and inventing a fourth colour scheme for axes would cost more than the collision does. Three things contain it:
[text]axis colours appear [strong]only[text] on the ground-plane axis lines and in the corner orientation

[text]Geometry is a light neutral rather than white, so that the specular range has somewhere to go and a lit face is distinguishable from a blown-out one.

[strong]Selection uses the same casing-and-core trick as wires[text], and for exactly the same reason: a selection outline has to be visible against both the near-black ground and the light geometry it surrounds.

rows=3 | [text]Layer ; [text]Width (screen space) ; [text]Colour ; [text]Contrast | [text]Casing ; [text]3 px ; [code]geometry.casing[text] [code]#0E1116 ; [text]9.35:1 against [code]geometry.surface | [text]Core ; [text]1.5 px ; [code]accent[text] [code]#A98BFF ; [text]7.04:1 against the casing, 6.15:1 against the ground

[text]The outline is drawn in [strong]screen space[text], so a selected object one metre away and one a hundred metres away have the same 1.5 px outline and both are findable. Selected surfaces additionally receive a 15% [code]accent[text] lighting tint, but the tint is never the only signal — the outline is authoritative.

[text]Points are drawn as 5 px screen-space discs in [code]geometry.edge[text] with a 1 px [code]geometry.casing[text] ring, because an unringed light dot vanishes the moment it lands on a light surface.
level=3 [text]8.4 Ghosted geometry: the one declared exception

[text]When geometry preview is isolated to the selection, everything else is ghosted to [code]geometry.ghost[text] [code]#616A79[text]. That is [strong]3.02:1 against the viewport ground[text] — perceivable — but only [strong]2.70:1 against `geometry.surface`[text], which is below 3.

[text]This is the single pairing in the document that sits under a floor, and it is unavoidable rather than sloppy: for ghosted geometry to be 3:1 below active geometry it would need a relative luminance of at most 0.113, and for it to be 3:1 above the ground it would need at least 0.140. No colour satisfies both. So the requirement is discharged differently:
[text]ghosted geometry is drawn [strong]edges-only, unshaded[text], while active geometry is shaded. The
[text]distinction is a [emphasis]rendering mode[text], not a contrast ratio, and it is absolute;
[text]ghosting is never the authoritative statement of what is previewed. The node's preview toggle
[text]in the graph is ([link->#77-frozen-preview-off-and-not-evaluated]§7.7[text]);
[strong]selected geometry is never ghosted[text], so nothing a user is acting on is ever in this state.
level=3 [text]8.5 Viewport overlays

[text]Everything drawn [emphasis]on top of[text] the scene is UI and is fully inside the contrast rules: the view-cube, the navigation bar, the units readout, the frame-rate counter, dimension text, and warning banners. They sit on E3 floating surfaces with their own fills — [code]text.primary[text] on [code]viewport.top[text] reads 15.12:1 — and never as bare text over unknown geometry.
level=2 [text]9. Typography
level=3 [text]9.1 Families

It is OFL-licensed and ships with the app, so a Linux build (ADR-0001) renders identically. Segoe UI is the fallback because it is on every Windows machine and has similar metrics, so a missing Inter degrades without reflowing the layout. | [text]Monospace ; [code]JetBrains Mono[text], [code]Cascadia Mono[text], [code]Consolas[text], [code]monospace ; [text]For the code block node and the script editor. JetBrains Mono has a slashed zero, visually distinct bracket families, and a taller-than-usual x-height at small sizes, which is what a nine-hour editing session needs. Cascadia ships with Windows Terminal and Consolas with Windows itself, so the fallback chain never reaches a default the user has not seen before.

[strong]Numeric fields use tabular figures[text] ([code]tnum[text]) — watch panels, sliders, coordinate readouts, property grids. Proportional digits make a value that updates during a drag appear to jitter sideways, which is both distracting and a genuine reading error when comparing a column of numbers.
level=3 [text]9.2 Scale

[text]At 100% UI scale. Every size scales with the OS display scale; none of them scale with canvas zoom except node text, which is dropped rather than scaled below 8 px ([link->#73-how-depth-degrades-with-zoom]§7.3[text]).

[strong]11 px is the floor.[text] Nothing in Spark is set smaller, at any scale, in any state.
level=3 [text]9.3 Weight on a dark ground

[text]Light text on a dark ground optically [strong]blooms[text]: the glyph appears heavier than the same weight does on a light ground, and thin strokes smear. So Spark uses one weight step lighter than a light theme would at every level:
[text]body is 400 and [strong]never 300[text] — a 300 weight at 13 px on [code]#23272F[text] loses stroke definition on
[text]any panel that is not perfectly calibrated;
[text]emphasis is 500 where a light theme would reach for 600;
[text]700 is not in the scale at all. Where a light theme would use 700, Spark uses 600 at the next
[text]size up.
[text]Weight is never the only signal for a state, because a weight change is worth roughly nothing at 11 px.
level=2 [text]10. Motion
level=3 [text]10.1 Tokens

rows=7 | [text]Token ; [text]Duration ; [text]Used for | [code]motion.instant ; [text]0 ms ; [text]Anything following the pointer directly: drags, pans, resizes, sliders | [code]motion.fast ; [text]90 ms ; [text]Hover in, ripple-free press feedback, port growth | [code]motion.base ; [text]140 ms ; [text]Hover out, selection, checkbox and toggle transitions | [code]motion.slow ; [text]220 ms ; [text]Popups, menus, tooltips appearing; elevation changes | [code]motion.deliberate ; [text]320 ms ; [text]Panel open and close, dock rearrangement, dialog entry | [code]motion.ambient ; [text]900 ms ; [text]The evaluating loop; the only repeating animation in the product

rows=4 | [text]Easing ; [text]Curve ; [text]Used for | [code]ease.standard ; [code]cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1) ; [text]Anything entering or changing state | [code]ease.exit ; [code]cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1, 1) ; [text]Anything leaving | [code]ease.linear ; [code]linear ; [text]Indeterminate progress only
[text]Hover in is [code]motion.fast[text]; hover out is [code]motion.base[text]. Faster in, slower out, so a pointer crossing a dense list does not strobe.
level=3 [text]10.2 On the canvas
[text]Motion is a frame-budget question here, not a taste question (ADR-0013 targets 2,000 nodes at 60 fps).
[text]Node hover is a [code]motion.fast[text] colour interpolation and nothing else — no elevation animation,
[text]no scale, no ripple.
[text]All per-node transitions are [strong]switched off entirely[text] when more than 400 nodes are visible or
[text]the zoom is below 60%. Below those thresholds state changes are instantaneous, which is also what a user zoomed out to survey a graph actually wants.
[text]Pan and zoom are [code]motion.instant[text] and follow the input device exactly. There is no smoothing,
[text]no inertia and no easing on a viewport transform; nothing makes a canvas feel worse than a canvas that keeps moving after you stop.
[text]The one exception is [emphasis]zoom to fit[text] and [emphasis]frame selection[text], which are [code]motion.deliberate[text] with
[code]ease.standard[text], because the user did not choose the destination and needs to see where they went.
level=3 [text]10.3 Reduced motion
[text]Spark honours the operating system's reduced-motion setting, and there is no in-app override that can turn it back on.
[text]When it is set:
[text]every duration above collapses to [code]motion.instant[text] [strong]except[text] [code]motion.deliberate[text] view
[text]transitions, which collapse to a 60 ms crossfade so that a jump-cut does not itself become disorienting;
[text]the evaluating loop becomes a static [code]accent[text] ring plus a [code]…[text] glyph — the state is still
[text]reported, only the movement is removed;
[text]indeterminate progress bars become a static striped fill that advances only when the underlying
[text]state actually changes.
[strong]No information is ever carried by motion alone[text], so reduced motion never removes a signal. That is a design constraint on every future feature, not a post-processing step.
level=2 [text]11. What this style is not allowed to do
[text]Concrete grounds for rejecting a change in review. Each one is a real failure mode of the style Spark has chosen, not a hypothetical.

[text]1. [strong]Text distinguished only by shadow.[text] If removing every shadow from a screenshot makes any text, icon or label harder to read, the screen is wrong. 2. [strong]Hover that lowers contrast.[text] Brightening a dark surface under light text, or darkening a bright fill under dark text. The direction is stated in [link->#51-the-hover-rule-and-why-it-inverts-the-usual-move]§5.1[text] and it has no exceptions. 3. [strong]Focus shown only by a glow.[text] Or only by a shadow, only by an elevation change, only by a colour change, or only on hover. The focus sandwich in [link->#6-keyboard-focus]§6[text] is the indicator; anything else is in addition to it. 4. [strong]Semantic state shown only by colour.[text] No error without a glyph and words, no warning without a glyph and words, no connection outcome without a cursor glyph. 5. [strong]A control boundary below 3:1 where the boundary is what identifies the control.[text] Depth so soft that an icon button becomes a smudge is a bug, and the fix is [code]border.control[text], not a larger blur. 6. [strong]Opacity used to signal state.[text] Not for disabled, not for not-evaluated, not for frozen, not for inactive tabs. Opacity reduces contrast by construction; the ladder, the desaturation and the flattening in [link->#55-disabled]§5.5[text] and [link->#77-frozen-preview-off-and-not-evaluated]§7.7[text] do the same jobs without it. 7. [strong]An accent or semantic tint behind text.[text] Selection uses a spine, a ring and a weight change ([link->#54-selected]§5.4[text]). Tints are for surfaces nobody reads. 8. [strong]A fifth elevation level, or a shadow with a blur radius outside {5, 6, 12, 16, 28}.[text] The set is fixed so the canvas can cache shadow sprites; a one-off blur is a frame-budget regression dressed as a design tweak. 9. [strong]A category colour used as a stroke, or a semantic colour used as a fill.[text] Principle 4 is what keeps a green node from being read as a passing node. 10. [strong]A pure black (`#000000`) shadow, or a surface below L\* 6 carrying elevation.[text] Both produce the punched-hole artefact described in [link->#28-the-hard-part-neumorphic-depth-on-a-dark-ground]§2.8[text]. 11. [strong]Text below 11 px, or a weight of 300 anywhere.[text] 12. [strong]Information carried by motion alone[text], which disappears entirely under reduced motion.

level=2 [text]14. Verifying this document

[text]Every ratio here comes from the sRGB relative-luminance formula in WCAG 2.2, with results truncated downward so a printed figure is never a rounded-up pass. Two checks belong in CI from M2, alongside the canvas benchmark:

[text]1. [strong]Palette check.[text] Parse the token table, recompute every pairing in [link->#4-contrast-rules-with-numbers]§4[text], and fail the build if any figure differs from the one printed here or falls below its floor. The tables are the fixture, exactly as [link->lacing.md]`concepts.lacing`[text]'s case table is the fixture for the engine. 2. [strong]Monotonicity check.[text] For every element in [link->#52-the-full-state-matrix]§5.2[text], assert that the contrast of every text token in the hover, pressed, selected and focused states is greater than or equal to its contrast at rest. This is Principle 2 as an assertion, and it is the one that catches the failure the style is prone to.
[text]If a future change makes a number in this document wrong, the correct response is to change the palette until the number is right again — not to edit the number.
